newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council in stalemate on new U.N. chief election.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council in stalemate on new U.N. chief election.

text.p: In defiance of the U.S. veto against the re-election of Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, African nations on Monday did not budge from supporting the 74-year-old Egyptian law professor.

The Security Council was stalemated after another meeting late on Monday in which no new names were presented. The United States cast its veto last Tuesday while the other 14 members supported Boutros-Ghali.

"We don't have any (new) list. It is composed of one person, Dr. Boutros-Ghali," said Botswana's U.N. ambassador Legwaila Joseph Legwaila, a member of the 15-seat Security Council that makes the decision.

British Ambassador Sir John Weston of Britain said it was time members had an "alternative basis to move forward." He said there was not much time before the General Assembly, which must approve any candidate, planned to recess on Dec. 17.
But Egypt's ambassador Nabil Elaraby said again that Boutros-Ghali was the sole candidate. Asked when another vote would be taken, he said "when there are 15."

A Western diplomat said it was extremely frustrating that no action could be taken because the Organisation of Africa Unity was "completely paralysed or unable to pronounce" on the subject. "It's not so difficult to come up with a list of 12 names."

Boutros-Ghali's term runs out at the end of this year, and the council has agreed to give priority to candidates from Africa on the grounds that if he is denied the second term given his predecessors, he should at least be followed by another African.

For many African countries, however, a united front was a mark of achievement that was difficult to obtain and may be difficult to sustain. Their first satisfaction, they say, was last Tuesday's 14-1 vote which diplomatically isolated the United States.

On the other hand, several Security Council nations would probably abstain if the vote on Boutros-Ghali was taken again, mainly because they do not believe the United States will change its mind. However, France, Russia and China, who also have veto power, are still backing Boutros-Ghali.

Some African nations have candidates they want to promote for the job. But they have been told to hold back on making a formal proposal until they are convinced there is no hope of negotiating at least a two-year extension for Boutros-Ghali.

Paul Biya, head of the Organisation of African Unity, is expected to telephone heads of African nations this week but no one expects a quick reply from 52 members before the council meets on the subject against on Friday.
Still in the background of the African strategy is France, which is expected to make sure no candidate seriously challenged Boutros-Ghali in the next week or so.

"The French want to prevent agreement on anyone else and then have members go on bended knee to (President Bill) Clinton and say there is no way forward except a compromise," said one Council envoy. So far there is no sign Washington would even consider a two-year compromise after Boutros-Ghali last spring turned down its offer of a one-year extension.

France's second strategy appears to be a delay until Francophone African nations decide on a candidate, a position criticised by the French daily Le Monde as dividing African nations unnecessarily and using the "impeccable mastery of the language of Moliere" as a prime criteria.

One plan to break the deadlock was for Council President Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia to present a list between now and the end of the month comprised of every candidate mentioned in the press or among diplomats.
The danger of this procedure for the Africans is that names from other regions would be mentioned. Asian candidates are next if line if no one can agree on an African nominee.

The United States says Boutros-Ghali has spent too little time streamlining the bodies, and the progress that has been made is due solely to U.S. pressure. More realistically, Washington says it cannot get the $1.4 billion it owes to the United Nations from a Republican-dominated Congress while he is in office.

But few diplomats believe there is a genuine major grievance against Boutros-Ghali. They say he and the United Nations have been made scapegoats for failures of U.S. policies in Bosnia and Somalia. Washington also received little support from its allies for unilaterally announcing the decision in the New York Times last June, without prior consultations.
